## Current authentication installations

The QFC server has two working, site-specific OAuth2 Proxy services. Both use the ***QFC-auth*** GitHub organization and team-based authorization. The former generic oauth2-proxy.service and oauth2-proxy.cfg were retired.

| Setting | GGPlot (static webpage) | Survey (Shiny app) |
|------------------|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| Website | /ggp/ | /survey/ |
| GitHub team | GGPlot | Survey |
| OAuth2 Proxy port | 4181 | 4182 |
| URL prefix | /oauth2-ggp | /oauth2-survey |
| Configuration file | /etc/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy-ggp.cfg | /etc/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy-survey.cfg |
| systemd service | oauth2-proxy-ggp.service | oauth2-proxy-survey.service |

Naming standard: use oauth2-proxy-\<site\>.cfg, oauth2-proxy-\<site\>.service, /oauth2-\<site\>, and a unique *oauth2_proxy*\<site\> cookie. Use a separate GitHub OAuth application and an unused localhost port for each site.

 

For the next example site (***biology***), this guide uses port 4183 because 4181 and 4182 are already assigned. Verify availability rather than assuming the port is free.

## Overview

This procedure adds GitHub Team authentication to an already deployed static website or Shiny application at <https://qfc.msu.edu>. Access is granted to members of the designated team in ***QFC-auth***.

 

**Prerequisites:**

Ubuntu server with Nginx with HTTPS, OAuth2 Proxy, systemd,

sudo access to the server

a deployed website

write access to the ***QFC-auth*** GitHub organization

 

These examples use ***micro*** to edit server configuration files and assume the website is ***https://qfc.msu.edu/biology/***.

## Server files added or modified

For each new protected website, two files are added to the server and one file is modified:

| Action | Server file | Purpose |
|-------|------------------------------|---------------------------------|
| Add | /etc/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy-biology.cfg | OAuth provider, GitHub organization/team, app credentials, callback, cookie, and unique local port. |
| Add | /etc/systemd/system/oauth2-proxy-biology.service | Runs and restarts the site-specific OAuth2 Proxy instance. |
| Modify | /etc/nginx/sites-available/default | Adds protected site routing, sign-in redirect, OAuth2 endpoints, and auth check within the HTTPS server block. |

## Create a GitHub team

In GitHub, open <https://github.com/orgs/QFC-auth/teams> and create a team named ***biology***. Add authorized users. Note: authorized users can be added at any time. Users must first join the QFC-auth organization. Use the team URL slug in the OAuth2 Proxy configuration; it may differ from the display name.

## Create a GitHub OAuth application

Under the ***QFC-auth*** organization, register a new OAuth application with the following values:

- **Application name:** QFC [Biology]{.replace-site}

- **Homepage URL:** https://qfc.msu.edu/biology/

- **Description**: Authentication for Biology

- **Authorization callback URL**: https://qfc.msu.edu/oauth2-biology/callback

 

Record the new Client ID and generate a Client Secret. [Never share the secret.]{.hl} Each site gets its own OAuth application and callback URL.

## Create the OAuth2 Proxy configuration

Each website requires its own OAuth2 Proxy configuration file. We will create a new file using ***biology*** as the example website.

### Select an available port {#sec-availablePort}

Each authenticated page on qfc.msu.edu will have its own port number starting with 4180.

 

This command will find the next available port

``` bash
for port in $(seq 4180 65535); do
    if ! ss -H -ltn "sport = :$port" | grep -q . &&
       ! sudo grep -RqE "http_address\s*=.*:$port([\"[:space:]]|$)" /etc/oauth2-proxy/; then
        echo "Available port: $port"
        break
    fi
done
```

Use the ***Available port*** number given after running this command. For these instructions, we will assume the port number is ***4183***.

### Generate a secret cookie {#sec-generateCookie}

Each website should have its own secret cookie. Run the following command:

``` bash
openssl rand -base64 32 | tr '+/' '-_'
```

Copy the generated value. You will use it for `cookie_secret` in the configuration below.

### Create the configuration file

Open the new file using ***micro***:

``` bash
sudo micro /etc/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy-«biology».cfg
```

Replace the highlighted values in the text below with:

- `biology` — Your website name and GitHub team slug

- `YOUR_CLIENT_ID` — Client ID from the GitHub OAuth application

- `YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET` — Client Secret from the GitHub OAuth application

- `YOUR_GENERATED_COOKIE_SECRET` — Value generated in section @sec-generateCookie

- `4183` — The port number found in @sec-availablePort

``` bash
provider = "github" 

github_org = "QFC-auth" 
github_team = "«biology»" 

client_id = "«YOUR_CLIENT_ID»" 
client_secret = "«YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET»" 

redirect_url = "https://qfc.msu.edu/oauth2-«biology»/callback" 

cookie_name = "_oauth2_proxy_«biology»" 
proxy_prefix = "/oauth2-«biology»" 

http_address = "127.0.0.1:«4183»" 

cookie_secret = "«YOUR_GENERATED_COOKIE_SECRET»" 
cookie_secure = true 
cookie_httponly = true 

email_domains = ["*"] 
whitelist_domains = ["qfc.msu.edu"] 
reverse_proxy = true 
trusted_proxy_ips = ["127.0.0.1/32", "::1/128"]
```

### Secure the configuration file

Restrict the configuration file to root access only:

``` bash
sudo chmod 600 /etc/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy-«biology».cfg
```

## Create and start the systemd service

Each website requires its own systemd service to run OAuth2 Proxy. We will create a new service using ***biology*** as the example website.

### Create the service file

Open a new file using ***micro***:

``` bash
sudo micro /etc/systemd/system/oauth2-proxy-«biology».service
```

Replace ***biology*** in the text below with your website name, paste the configuration, and save the file:

``` bash
[Unit]
Description=OAuth2 Proxy - «Biology»
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target
 
[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/oauth2-proxy --config=/etc/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy-«biology».cfg
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
 
[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

### Reload systemd

Notify ***systemd*** that a new service has been created:

``` bash
sudo systemctl daemon-reload 
```

### Enable and start the service

Enable the service to start automatically when the server boots, and start it immediately:

``` bash
sudo systemctl enable --now oauth2-proxy-«biology» 
```

### Verify the service is running

Check the server status

``` bash
sudo systemctl status oauth2-proxy-«biology» --no-pager
```

The output should include:

```         
Active: active (running)
```

Confirm the service is active before continuing.

## Configure Nginx

Nginx controls how visitors access websites on the QFC server. We need to configure Nginx to:

1.  Identify websites that require authentication.

2.  Check whether a visitor is authorized through OAuth2 Proxy.

3.  Redirect unauthorized visitors to GitHub authentication.

4.  Serve the website after successful authentication.

 

Nginx configuration differs slightly between **static websites** (such as Quarto websites) and **Shiny applications**.

### Open the Nginx configuration file

\<create a backup first...\>

``` bash
sudo micro /etc/nginx/sites-available/default
```

The file contains two `server` blocks:

- The first redirects HTTP requests to HTTPS.

- The second handles HTTPS requests and contains the website configurations.

 

**All new configuration should be added inside the second `server` block**, before the final `location /` block that redirects unmatched requests to the main QFC website.

 

For each new website, we will add a section containing the website configuration and its authentication endpoints.

### Configure the protected website

Choose **one** of the following configurations, depending on the type of website.

#### Static website (e.g., Quarto, HTML)

Use this configuration for a static website whose HTML files are stored on the server.

 

For this example, we assume:

- Website URL: <https://qfc.msu.edu/biology/>

- Website directory: /var/www/html/biology/docs/

- OAuth2 Proxy prefix: /oauth2-biology

 \
Add the following configuration (replace ***biology*** with the website):

``` bash
# ======================================================== 
# «BIOLOGY» — PROTECTED STATIC WEBSITE 
# ======================================================== 
# GitHub organization: QFC-auth 
# GitHub team: «»biology 
# Website directory: /var/www/html/«biology»/docs/ 
# ======================================================== 

location /«biology»/ { 
    auth_request /oauth2-«biology»/auth; 
    error_page 401 = @oauth2_«biology»_signin; 
    
    alias /var/www/html/«biology»/docs/; 
    index index.html; 
} 

# Redirect /«biology» to /«biology»/ 
location = /«biology» { 
    return 301 /«biology»/; 
}
```

**How this works:**

- `location /biology/` identifies the website being protected.

- `auth_request` asks OAuth2 Proxy whether the visitor is authorized.

- `error_page 401` redirects unauthorized visitors to the sign-in process.

- `alias` identifies the directory containing the website files.

- `index index.html` specifies the default page.

- The second location block ensures that `/biology` redirects to `/biology/`.

 

**Important:** The `alias` path must match the actual location of the website files. For a Quarto website, this will typically be the directory containing the rendered HTML files.

#### Shiny application

Use this configuration for an application running through Shiny Server.

 

For this example, we assume:

- Application URL: <https://qfc.msu.edu/biology/>

- Shiny Server: port 3838

- Shiny application path: /biology/

- OAuth2 Proxy prefix: /oauth2-biology

 

Add the following configuration (replace ***biology*** with the website):

``` bash
# ======================================================== 
# BIOLOGY — PROTECTED SHINY APPLICATION 
# ======================================================== 
# GitHub organization: QFC-auth 
# GitHub team: biology 
# Shiny Server: 127.0.0.1:3838 
# ======================================================== 
location /biology/ { 
    auth_request /oauth2-biology/auth; 
    error_page 401 = @oauth2_biology_signin; 
    
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3838/biology/; 
    proxy_http_version 1.1; 
    
    proxy_set_header Host $host; 
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr; 
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; 
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; 
    
    # Required for Shiny WebSocket connections 
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade; 
    proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade"; 
} 
    
# Redirect /biology to /biology/ 
location = /biology { 
    return 301 /biology/; 
}
```

**How this differs from a static website:**

- `proxy_pass` forwards requests to Shiny Server instead of serving HTML files directly.

- `proxy_http_version 1.1` enables HTTP/1.1 communication with Shiny Server.

- The `Upgrade` and `Connection` headers support WebSocket connections, which Shiny uses for interactive communication.

- The remaining proxy headers pass information about the original request to Shiny Server.

 

The Shiny application must already be deployed and accessible through Shiny Server

### Configure the authentication endpoints

**This section is identical for static websites and Shiny applications.**

 

Add the following blocks after the website configuration.

 

These blocks connect Nginx to the OAuth2 Proxy instance created in Steps 3 and 4.

For this example, OAuth2 Proxy uses port `4183` – replace that with the actual port number

``` bash
# ======================================================== 
# BIOLOGY — GITHUB AUTHENTICATION 
# ======================================================== 
# OAuth2 Proxy service: oauth2-proxy-biology 
# OAuth2 Proxy port: «4183»
# OAuth2 Proxy prefix: /oauth2-biology 
# ======================================================== 
# Redirect unauthenticated visitors to sign-in 
location @oauth2_«biology»_signin { 
    return 302 /oauth2-«biology»/sign_in?rd=$scheme://$host$request_uri; 
} 

# Forward OAuth2 requests to OAuth2 Proxy 
location /oauth2-«biology»/ { 
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:«4183»; 
    
    proxy_set_header Host $host; 
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr; 
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; 
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; 
} 

# Check whether visitors are authenticated 
location = /oauth2-«biology»/auth { 
    internal; 
    
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:«4183»/oauth2-«biology»/auth; 
    
    proxy_pass_request_body off; 
    proxy_set_header Content-Length ""; 
    
    proxy_set_header X-Original-URI $request_uri; 
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr; 
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; 
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    proxy_set_header Host $host; 
}
```

**How these blocks work:**

Sign-in redirect

- The `@oauth2_biology_signin` block sends unauthorized visitors to the OAuth2 Proxy sign-in page.

- The `rd` parameter records the original URL so users can return to the requested page after authentication.

 

OAuth2 Proxy endpoints

- The `/oauth2-biology/` block forwards authentication-related requests to the OAuth2 Proxy service running on port 4183.

- These requests include the GitHub OAuth callback and authentication cookies.

 

Authentication check

- The `/oauth2-biology/auth` block allows Nginx to ask OAuth2 Proxy whether the current visitor is authorized.

- The `internal` directive prevents visitors from accessing this endpoint directly while allowing Nginx to use it for authorization checks.

### Save the test the configuration file

To test the configuration file

``` bash
sudo nginx -t
```

If the configuration is valid, you should see:

``` bash
nginx: the configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf syntax is ok 
nginx: configuration file /etc/nginx/nginx.conf test is successful
```

If an error is reported, return to the configuration file and correct it before proceeding.

 

[Do not reload Nginx until the configuration test succeeds.]{.hl}

### Reload nginx

Apply the new configuration:

``` bash
sudo systemctl reload nginx
```

Reloading Nginx applies the changes without stopping the server.

 

The new website should now require GitHub authentication.

### Verify the website

Open a private browser window and visit: `https://qfc.msu.edu/biology/`

 

You should be redirected to GitHub authentication.

 

After signing in, users belonging to the appropriate GitHub team should be able to access the website.

 

Users who are not members of the team should be denied access.

 

For Shiny applications, also verify that the application responds correctly to user input.

 

Detailed authentication testing is covered in the next step.

## Validate and test

``` bash
sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx
```

Only reload Nginx if `nginx -t` succeeds. Open https://qfc.msu.edu/ in a private browser window and test all three cases: (1) signed-out user is redirected to GitHub; (2) QFC-auth member on the [biology]{.replace-site} team is allowed; (3) organization member not on the team is denied. A nonmember of QFC-auth should also be denied.

 

For troubleshooting:

``` bash
sudo journalctl -u oauth2-proxy-biology -n 50 --no-pager
```

## Manage access in GitHub

To grant or revoke access, add or remove users from the [biology]{.replace-site} team in ***QFC-auth***. No Nginx or OAuth2 Proxy edits are required for routine membership changes. Existing authenticated sessions may remain valid until authorization is checked again or the session expires.

## Quick reference

| GitHub organization | No change |
|----|----|
| GitHub team | Create one per site |
| OAuth application | Create one per site |
| OAuth2 Proxy configuration | Create one .cfg per site |
| systemd | Create one service per site |
| Nginx | Add protected site, sign-in, proxy, and auth-check routes |
| Website content | No changes required for an existing static site |

## Maintenance and cleanup checks

Confirm that only the intended services are enabled and the old configuration is no longer referenced. Do not remove either active service or its configuration file.

```{=html}
<pre class="config-block"><code>sudo systemctl list-unit-files &#x27;oauth2-proxy*&#x27;
sudo ls -l /etc/oauth2-proxy/
sudo grep -RnI -E &#x27;QFCatMSU|github_users|oauth2-proxy\.cfg|oauth2-proxy\.service&#x27; /etc/nginx /etc/oauth2-proxy /etc/systemd/system 2&gt;/dev/null</code></pre>
```

Expected active files: oauth2-proxy-ggp.cfg and oauth2-proxy-survey.cfg; expected services: oauth2-proxy-ggp.service and oauth2-proxy-survey.service. The grep should return no matches after cleanup. Nginx is configured in /etc/nginx/sites-available/default (usually linked from sites-enabled/default).

Before modifying Nginx, back up /etc/nginx/sites-available/default; always run sudo nginx -t before reloading. Use micro for edits. When pasting large configuration blocks, disable autoindent in micro to avoid accumulating indentation.
